utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see, Your Honours, that the next witness is being brought into court. I should indicate that he is Milazim Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stamp. Good afternoon, Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, could you start by introducing yourself, by telling us your full name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: My name is Milazim Thaqi. I was born on the 14th of July, 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 where did you live?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: During the year 1998 and 1999, I used to live in the village of Broje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, it belongs to the municipality of Skenderaj in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you live with your family there at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many family members were there that you lived with?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: At the time, there were seven of us living in Broje. The others lived abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You had a wife and children, I take it, living with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were the ages of the children, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: From 15 and under.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to tell us briefly about the prevailing conditions in the area of your village in 1998, 1998. Did you and your family remain living in your village in that year all the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: From March the 5th, 1998, we spent a whole month, that is, me and my family, including my mother who was ill; the others, however, went away to the direction of Vojnik. They went because there were Serbian forces about 500 [as interpreted] metres away from where we used to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just tell us again what happened in 1998 leading to the movement of yourself and your family from where you lived.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: On March the 5th Serbian police and army forces came aboard tanks and other vehicles and they forced us to abandon our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How did they force you? What happened that caused you to abandon your village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I never came into contact with them, but they came and installed themselves about 50 metres away from our house, they beat up certain other people who they met, which means that the rest of us were afraid that the same would befall us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did they come 50 metres away from your house or 500 metres?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: 50 metres away from my house. There were lots of them. They shot and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So just tell us who left your village.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The entire village left on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And about when did your family return to the village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We returned on June the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now I would like to take you to the year 1999 and the period immediately after the commencement of the NATO intervention into Kosovo. At the time of the NATO intervention, where were you and your family living?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The day that NATO arrived in Kosova I was in my house in the village of Broje, that is on the 24th of March. Two days later we left the village and went to Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who left the village and went to Izbica two days later?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The whole village. I just can't say their names. Everybody went. The place was left empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about your family, how many members of your family left?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: All of us, all seven of us, with a tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why did your family, yourself, and the other villagers abandon your village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Why? Because we saw what massacres they'd carried out in Racak, Prekaze, Likoshan, Qirez, and so on and so forth. I can't enumerate them all here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, in just two sentences explain to me what you mean by what massacres they carried out. And just tell me who carried out these massacres, and what do you mean by massacre?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I'm talking about crimes committed by the Yugoslav police and army, including the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And how did you come to learn about these crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: How we came to learn about them? After the Racak massacre and the one in Qirez and Prekaze. I went and saw the places. I saw them with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on the 26th of March when you left or prior to that day, were there Serbian forces or Yugoslav forces in the vicinity of your village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yeah, all the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Prior to the time you left, were there Kosovo Verification Mission members there verifying the conduct of the Serb authorities? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They used to be there, yes, but I think they left before Serbian forces came.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the massacres that you -- you are speaking about, can you remember when, approximately when, they took place?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. The Racak massacre occurred on January the 15th; Qirez and Likoshan on the 28th of February; on March the 5th, it's Prekaze, and I'm talking about 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the Racak massacre of January 15th; Cirez and Likosane on the 28th of February, is that 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the Racak massacre occur in the same year of the NATO intervention or a different year?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, no. It happened on January the 15th, 1998, whilst the NATO intervention came on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the -- what you described as the massacres in Cirez and Likosane on the 28th of February, do you recall if that was 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The Racak massacre and the one in Prekaze and Qirez all occurred in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, after the NATO intervention commenced on the 24th of March, 1999, were there any movements of Serbian or Yugoslav forces in the vicinity of your village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The whole area was occupied, including my village and the adjoining village and so on and so forth. The Yugoslav and Serbian police and army were installed there all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When were they installed there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They were in my village, in Broje; and Jashanice; there were others in Rakinice and in the surrounding areas. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. At around or about when did these forces arrive in the vicinity of your village and Jashanice?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They reached Jashanice on the 25th of March, after the NATO attacks; on the 26th they reached Broje, Turicevc, and other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you left your village on the 26th of March, did you come in contact with any of these forces that had arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, because they had not reached that point yet. We left before they were able to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, earlier you told us that you arrived with other villagers in the -- in Izbica --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Izbica. Thank you very much. Could you just tell us, the people who travelled from your village to Izbica, what was the composition of the group of people? And I'm talking about -- ages and sex of the people who travelled with you to Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I can say that there were people who were, for instance, up to 103 years of age, the elderly; there were young people amongst them; there were people of 50 or 30; there were women who had children of 5 or 6 months, i.e., there were people from across the age factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you arrived in the area of Izbica, where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: When we arrived in Izbice, I went to Gani Rama's house in Izbice, and that's where I stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about the larger group of villagers from Izbica, where did they go to?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: On the 27th, before the massacre, they left in the course of the night on tractors and all other vehicles to the village of Tushille, which was considered to be out of danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you arrived at --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I stayed in Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. When you arrived at Izbica, did you see people there in the area of Izbica --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Izbice, sorry again. Did you see people gathered there anywhere in the vicinity of Izbice?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Oh, yes, a lot. I didn't count them, but there were certainly between 10.000 and 12.000 including women, children, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where were the people gathered?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Most of them slept out in the open, on board tractors; some others went in houses if there was enough space inside. However, at about 8.00 in the morning everybody was asked to gather outside to be in a way together in anticipation of any kind of massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 8.00 on which morning? Tell me the date of that morning, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It was on the 27th. It was a Saturday, and it rained during that night. So this was the morning of the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the people who were gathered outside, from which villages were they or did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I can say that they came from 15 or 20 of the surrounding villages, and they all converged there. There were all kinds of people. There were groups of four to five families, of ten families together, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remember some of the main villages that they came from?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. They came from Gllareve, Jashanice, Likoc, Tejice, from Kline in Skenderaj municipality, Broje, Vojnik, Turiqevc, the lower Kopiliq, and so on and so forth. There were lots of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, while you were gathered in the vicinity of Izbica, could you at any time observe or see what if anything was happening in the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, there's nothing, just noise -- the noises. Because it's -- that -- it's at a lower altitude. There were hills all around and that's where we were. We knew nothing about it. We saw armed people but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What sort of noises were you hearing?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The noise of tanks, of lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And after you arrived at Izbica, could you see or did you manage to see into any of the villages that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll just repeat the question. Did you manage to see into any of the villages from which the people had arrived while you were at Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want me to mention them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I want you to tell us if you saw anything in these villages and what you saw.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We saw nothing during the journey; however, when we arrived we found Hasan who came from Gllareve and who had survived that massacre. There were people from Vojnik, someone called Sheremet Krasniqi, Musli Kotorri, there were many, many people. I can't recall their names at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What -- while you were at Izbica, what happened to these villages that the people had left?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They came from their own villages. The village of Izbice had -- was a bit freer. And in terms of staying they used to tell us that Serbian forces had not done anything wrong in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's in Izbica, but do you know if anything happened in the villages from which these people left to go to Izbica after they had left?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In Jashanice where the check-point was there were forces that had come from all sides, Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did these villages remain intact or were they damaged in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: All of them were levelled to the ground. The houses were all burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you observe this while you were in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: After we escaped death, I saw this with my own eyes because we proceeded on foot when we survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. I'd like to show you a map of the area just to get us oriented, and I'd like you to just point out where these villages are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, could I put on the screen P615. And I want -- if we could find page 11. I think it's page 16, let's try 16 because -- and it is the page after that. I'm so sorry. And if we could just zoom in a little bit to the top or let's -- to the top and a little to the right. And perhaps if we scroll down a little bit. Please stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you locate Izbica on the map as it is, Mr. Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I cannot see it very well. Here is Broje. I can't see it really. Turiqevc, Broje, Vojnik, Izbice, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's start with your village, Broje, could you mark that with a 1 or with a 1 just below it.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Here is number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you help him to hold that pen properly, Mr. Usher, so he could mark it. No, I don't think he's holding the pen properly. If you could help him to hold the pen. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you put a number 2 on Izbica. That is where you travelled to.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Number 2, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And if we could identify some of the surrounding villages. You'll see Vojnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you put a number 3 under that village.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Here is Vojnik. Klladernice, lower Kopiliq number 4, here number 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, you're going too fast. Lower -- or Gornje Obilic you marked a number 4 under it, you were there --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, it's not Obilic but Kopiliq. There are two Kopiliqs: Upper and lower Kopiliq. And here is Turiqevc, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you mark a number 7 for Belice?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Kopiliq.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, maybe I have the pronunciation wrong. Belice or Belica.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, no. Here is Kopiliq i Ulet or lower Kopiliq, it's near Turiqevc.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Stop there, stop there, Mr. Thaqi. You see where you have Izbica marked?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, Vojnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, just above Izbica to the left do you see a village there looking like Belice. Maybe I have the pronunciation wrong.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Belice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Did refugees also leave from that village to go towards Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This village was inhabited by Serbs. The Serbs from Belice, Polan, Leqina, and Peje were the ones who did what they did in the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but what I'm asking is did the Serbs from that village or from Polane, were they part of the refugee group, were they forced out of their villages?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They didn't leave their villages. They joined the Serb forces and the paramilitaries that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the villages you've marked with a number 4 or number 5, were people forced out of those villages or people from those villages joined the refugees that went to Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, from all these villages they came to Izbice. They also came from other villages, many other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I tender this and ask that it be received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00819, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you describe the place where you and the other villagers gathered together in Izbica when you were told to come out into the open?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Shall I do it with a pen?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. Just tell us the -- the place where you gathered. Was it an open field or was it in a particular area of Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It was an open field, a meadow, that's where we all gathered. People, tractors, horse-drawn carts, the cemetery is nearby the location where we were all gathered. It was in the middle of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P002 -- sorry, 65 number 00244. This is a document, Your Honours, which had been premarked, I should indicate that to the Court. I have been trying to find an unmarked copy. I don't know if we received in our possession an unmarked copy of this. Is it -- of this aerial photograph, but I will not ask him anything about the markings. Could the -- could this be expanded as much as possible or is that as far as it could go? Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you to ignore those markings and just -- if we have a blue pen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should only like to ask Mr. Stamp to give us the source for this photograph if possible, who made it, and any other details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's already an exhibit, Mr. Djordjevic. Can we be reminded of any of those matters, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think it is yet an exhibit. This is a document that the OTP received from one of the agencies that went into Kosovo in 1999, an aerial photograph of many of the places. On some of these documents we are able to locate unmarked copies. This is one that was marked, and we haven't been able to find an unmarked copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. So you don't have any specific knowledge at the moment of the date of the photography or who it was that took the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not specifically. I could just add, Your Honours, that I will just ask the witness to identify certain places and if the photograph depicts his memory of certain basic areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. The witness is going to be asked, Mr. Djordjevic, whether he can identify what is shown in this photograph. If not, it goes nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all I wanted to say that this is certainly not an exhibit, as my colleague Mr. Stamp has just said; and second, I see some lines here, I see mark A, B, C, I see mark D, and E, and perhaps F. So this is already marked and I would not be very happy if this should be used for something that the witness would be asked to mark now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We heard from Mr. Stamp, Mr. Djordjevic, that he cannot find an unmarked copy, and he does not propose to ask the witness anything about the markings that do appear on it. And we -- I think we should proceed with the questioning and see whether there is any problem presented by the existing marks. Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Thaqi, are you able to identify the area that this aerial photograph depicts?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which area is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This is Izbice village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you -- or may I ask you this: Can you identify places on this picture as it is or would you prefer if it was oriented differently, if it was turned, if it was reversed, and turned upside down?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It would be better if you turn it upside down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you mean upside down or merely 90 degrees?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 180 degrees, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It needs to be turned another quarter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's okay like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What part of Izbica is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This is the road coming from Vojnik, and we were gathered here, in this field, in this meadow, which is in the middle of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like you to just put an X in the middle of the meadow as you see it where you and the other people were gathered. Small X.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on the morning of the 28th of March, 1999, at about 9.30, where were you and the other villagers gathered?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: On the 28th of March, we were all here on both sides of the road in this open field. People from all the villages nearby that had gathered there with all their belongings, tractors, and other vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That morning while you were there, did anything happen to the people there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That morning we had some breakfast, if you can call it so, some ate, some didn't, before 9.00. At around 9.30 the Serb forces came and separated us from the women and the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like you to take it step by step. The first Serbian forces that you saw arrive there, how many were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I didn't count them, but they were about 80 if not more, there in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When the Serb forces first approached the people in the village, where did you first see them?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I first saw them after we had breakfast. They set a haystack on fire near a pear tree, and I went closer to them just to hear what they were saying. They were asking for money. They asked for 1.000 Deutschemarks if we wanted our houses and tractors safe. I only had 30 Deutschemarks on me, and that's what I gave them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you -- what language did they speak in?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Serbian, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You understand Serbian? Do you speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I understand Serbian because I served in the Yugoslav Army in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. When you saw the Serbian forces set fire to the pear tree, how many of them did you see there doing that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: There were three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They had police clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Describe that a little bit more for me. What colour and if any patterns were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The colour of the Yugoslav police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Any particular pattern in the colour?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Some had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The three men that you saw in the Serbian police uniform, were they armed with weapons; and if so, what type of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, they had automatic guns, weapons, and also had hand-grenades on their belts, knives, ammunition belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I'm just asking you for the time being in relation to those three. What was the colour of the uniforms they wore?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The colour of the Yugoslav police uniforms, one of them I think had a camouflage uniform and the others that sort of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you name the colour?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: You see here where the forest is -- I'm not touching it, no, I just want to show you the colour. I'm not touching it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you able to tell me in a word what colour?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: If I'm to describe the colour with a word, it's a sort of green colour. I don't know how you call it, blue/green.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that there were also at some point in time 80 other policemen in the vicinity of the meadow where these people were gathered. Firstly, were these policemen also armed, and what were the weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The three policemen came first. Some five minutes later the others came, as if they just cropped out from earth. That's how suddenly they came out. Some of them had automatic weapons, some had machine-guns, some had hand-grenades, knives, all sorts of weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you describe how the men were dressed?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The police had the uniform I described earlier, this blue/green uniform. There were soldiers who had Yugoslav uniforms, and some had paramilitary uniforms. They had black scarves on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say soldiers had Yugoslav uniforms, can you describe further to me further what you saw them wearing which caused you to say they had Yugoslav uniforms. Just describe what you saw them wearing.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Because they were familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Describe the uniform, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It was the colour of the grass, the army uniform, that is. The others, the paramilitaries, had a similar uniform but with a patterned -- with mixture of colours, a camouflaged pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "paramilitaries," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They were paramilitaries, they were not regular soldiers. They called them Chetniks or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And apart from the black scarves you said they wore on their heads, did you notice that helped you to distinguish them or identify them?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, only that they had knives and other kinds of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether or not there were more soldiers at the time outside of the meadows in the woodland around Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: There were many soldiers around the hills. As to their numbers, I can't say. But we -- we were not able to see anything. We were able to see, you know, the tracks made by the lorries and so on and so forth, but there must have been lots of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. That morning when you saw these 80-plus policemen, some soldiers, paramilitaries, could you just tell us what if anything they did or said to the people gathered in the field.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: There in the field we were separated from the women and the children, and they told the women and the children to raise [Realtime transcript read in error "brace"] their three fingers, they kept shouting, whilst they -- to the rest of us they put us in groups of four one by one, they insulted us and told us to remove our hats, and they kept asking, Where is America? Where is Clinton? Where is Thaqi? Let them come and take you out of this situation. And they did this three times in a row.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said we were separated from the women and the children. How many men were separated from the women and the children approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Roughly there were 157 altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what generally in a ballpark sense were the ages of these men?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The men ranged from 86 years of age to around 47, 45 and above, 50s, in their 50s, 60s.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said they told the women and children to -- and I think there's a -- excuse me, Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think there's a mistake -- I see a mistake in the transcript at line 17, page 18. It says to "brace their three fingers." I think it should be "raise their three fingers."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, you said they told the women and the children to raise their three fingers. What did that signify?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This sign indicates that this is Serbia. That is the reason shy some raised their fingers, some didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did they tell the women and the children what would happen to them or where they were going to?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They told them to raise their three fingers and that they would all be sent to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you said in respect to the men that they put you in groups, did they let you remain standing, or did they put you in another position when they put you in groups?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They asked us to sit four -- in groups of four, one behind the other, on the side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, if you could get back to the document we have in front of you. Could you mark with a number 1 the area where you and the men were put to sit on the side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, it's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that their -- they told you to take off your hats and throw them down. Is that the type of hat that you're presently wearing in court?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is it called?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: In Albanian it is called "Plis," it's a skull cap. There were others who had black hats. They all had to take them off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is this a traditional headwear of Albanian men, of Kosovo Albanian men?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This is part of the national costume. It only belongs to Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did any of these policemen do anything to you in particular while you sat there on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, no, they didn't say anything. They told some people, You belong to the KLA, to some others they didn't say anything, but they kept insulting us all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And generally, do you remember the nature, the general nature, of these insults?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They told you do so and so to your mother to all the Albanians. One of them kicked me, one of the policemen, before I was made to sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did these policemen or did these men gathered there appear to have a leader?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you describe him and tell us what he was doing? Start by describing him. Let's go step by step.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing a soldier's uniform. He was of medium height, 1.65 centimetres -- metres. He was -- his face was longish. His nose was a bit crooked. He had two radios.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the colour of his uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It was the green grass colour of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did he use the radios while he was there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just describe to us, if you can, what he did while he was there, in particular what he did to cause you to determine that he was the leader?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: He was their leader because he kept issuing orders to the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, fully armed, up to the teeth as they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm speaking about that one particular person who you said was the leader. Was he armed? With what? Or what was he armed with? What weapon did he have?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: He had a pistol, a knife, the two communications equipment, bombs, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you notice whether or not he had insignia, an insignia or insignias on his sleeve or sleeves?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I was not brave enough to look him right in the eye, but I think he had that insignia on the right arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he do anything in respect to the group of Albanian refugees that were gathered there? Or did he give any instructions in relation to what was to be done to the group?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, no. It was only the police who went in the midst of the women folk and kept looking for men to separate them, but I did not see him at that stage. He only issued the orders afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us what orders he issued in respect to the Albanian folk that were there.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Not to the Albanians --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: -- but to the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Go on, tell us what he told them to do, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: He told them in Serbian, Everybody knows their own duty, you know what you have to do, and you have to start immediately. This is what I was able to hear myself because they were right next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When he told them that they knew their duty and they were to start immediately, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We were just in the middle of the road, seated. One of them told us to stand and so he pointed from this point to that point, all of you have got to stand up, which we did. And we proceeded to the left and upwards in the middle of the field, and he said that we were to be sent towards Peje, the others towards Kline. We kept asking how on earth? How can we go up into the mountains with no buses, nothing whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So when this person or one of these men spoke to you, did you do anything after you stood up?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: He issued orders to us. We did not speak to him. We stood up in rows of four. He said, No, you should go two abreast. So we went two abreast and proceeded upwards in the direction of the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did all of the men who had been seated there, where you showed us, go with you or were the men separated?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No. The first group -- in fact, I wasn't brave enough even to look. I just turned very briefly, my head very briefly, because he kept the automatic gun trained on us. So I was with the first group. There were 33 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where did the first group go to?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The first group was sent alongside the mountain near a water creek; and he shouted to us in Serbian to stop, which we did; and he said, Turn left, and we did. He ordered us to kneel, which we did, then he started shooting. I lay prostrate onto the ground and to this day, I don't know how it occurred, but there were two corpses on top of me, and I stayed underneath for 40 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Just a minute. I'd like you to go back if we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if we could go back to the aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- and put a 2, if you can identify the place where your group of, approximately, I think you said, 33 men were taken.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Number 2, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The letter A -- or is it a 1? In any case, it comes at the end of the line where we also have an A. So now we're in the situation that I tried to indicate at the outset. If you have a look at it, the end of the line where the A stands is precisely along the same line where the witness put the -- had put the mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I quite agree, and if you are concerned that one is guiding the other that should be dealt with in cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many members of the Serbian forces that were at the field that day went with your group of men to the area where this shooting occurred? And I'm just asking you about how many you saw going there with you.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: There was one single person who had a machine-gun of 100 millimetres, and he sent us to the foot of the mountain. There were 33 of us. Three of us survived and live to this day; the others all perished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This person who sent you to the foot of the mountain, was he policeman, soldier, or paramilitary? That is the one you just described with the 100-millimetre machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This one had the same uniform which was the green grass colour but it was in camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say whether or not he was a policeman, soldier, or paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It looked like a policeman to me. I wasn't brave enough to look him right in the eye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying a policeman but in a green grass colour uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was like the grass, the colour of the grass, but in camouflage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When he started shooting -- well, tell us, in which direction did he fire, and about how long did the shooting last?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: He turned his back towards us. I don't think it lasted more than half a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. You said -- I just see here -- you said he turned his back towards you. That is the interpretation I have. Could I just ask you again. When he fired, did he fire in your direction?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: He told us to stop in Serbian, turn to the -- turn left, kneel, which we did. Before we were able to kneel, he started shooting with his weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When he started shooting, were you facing him, was your side to him, or was your back to him at the time when he started shooting?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We had our backs, we were facing the creek, the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What happened to you and the other men during the course of the shooting and immediately after? Just describe to us in your own words what happened.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: He was still there waiting, and he spoke in Serbian and he said, This one is still breathing. And he shouted some abuse. I thought it was meant for me, but he shot with a pistol in the direction of someone over there, I don't know who it was. After that, he left and the second group arrived near a pear tree. I was able to hear the shooting because we were about 20 to 25 metres away, but they were not able to see us because it was a hilly terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that when he started fighting you lay prostrate and there were two corpses on top of you and you stayed underneath for 40 minutes. Do you know who lay on top of you, the corpses?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it was Uke Uka Thaqi from Broje. The whole of his -- of the top of his head had been blown off. His brains were all over me, some of them in my pocket; and the other one was Isuf Zezeqa Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said you heard shooting in the vicinity or from the direction of the pear tree while you lay there. Is that correct? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long did you lay there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: 40 minutes. The third group was brought about 20 metres away from where I was. They killed everyone with the exception of one single person, Hajzir Kotorri, who stood up walking in the direction of the mountain. However, there were others who were in the tractor road in the middle of the mountain who told him to stop in Serbian, he did not, and so he was shot straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You are telling us about shooting of other men. Did you actually see this while you were lying under the other two men, or did you hear about this later on?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: When I was lying prostrate, I dared not lift my head; however, 40 minutes later Demush Behrami died and he shouted as he did so, I did the same; and then Sheqir, who came from Kotor, touched me and asked who I was, I said I'm Milazim from Broje. At some distance Qallapeki did not speak to us at all, and I ask him at one moment whether he was able to climb the mountain --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Thaqi, I don't think you are focusing on what I'm asking you. The other shootings that you mentioned of other groups, did you see the shooting at the time while you laid there or did you discover about that later on?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I did not see them with my own eyes. I only heard the shooting because I dared not get up --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I only saw it later because we were the ones to bury them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. We will get to that later.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. For the time being, let's stick to what you actually saw and heard.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said as you laid there Demush Behrami died and then --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Demush Behrami from Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And Sheqir touched you and asked you who you were. Sheqir what? What was Sheqir's --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Sheqir Kotorri and Jetish Qallapeki, they were the two who survived and who live to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. After you lay there, did you, Sheqir, and the other one go anywhere? Did you get up and leave?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We crawled on the side of the mountain. This is a tractor road in there -- in fact, there were members of the army or paramilitaries or the police. I did not see them; however, we heard them. So we stopped for about ten minutes, after which they set off in the direction of the village of Turjan which they set fire to. When we crossed the road, we saw them wearing Yugoslav Army boots. They dropped empty Marlboro cigarette boxes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You crawled on the side of the mountain you said. Could we return to the photograph, and I'd like you to place an arrow showing us the direction that you travelled yourself and the two other men to escape.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Look at -- sorry, look at the aerial photograph, identify the area you travelled to escape, and just put an arrow to show us what was the path you took to escape.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We went uphill in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the witness, Your Honours, for the record, drew something like an arrow pointing towards the bottom part of the map where there is a dark green area of foliage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is commencing close to the number 2, I would add for the transcript. We have gone over time, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will need to have our first break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the map -- could the aerial photograph as marked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's what I was leading to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The map -- the aerial photograph that has been marked will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00820, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I would mention we have received it subject to our assessment in due course of the premarking and its consequence, if any, for the evidence of the witness. We will have our first break now and resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My apologies. I was delayed on another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe as we adjourn I could indicate that with us in court is a new intern, Ms. Yordanka Nedyalkova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down, Mr. Thaqi. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you left, Mr. Thaqi, you indicated to us that you escaped with two other men into the hills adjacent to where the shooting occurred, but we didn't get the names of the men fully. Could you just tell us their names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we got the first name of one with the village where he's from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did, Your Honour. It was corrected after the last time I saw the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About what time of the day did you and these two men escape into the woods?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, after surviving, we had a chat amongst ourselves. I told Sheqir, You get up and lead us because Izbica and Vojnik are adjacent to each other and I told him that he knew the area better. And he said he did not know even where he was. I only know that I'm talking to yourself, which means that I was then in the lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What hour of the day was this?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: When we had reached almost half the height of the mountain it was about 11.15 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were in the mountains, did you meet up with other survivors who were among the men in the field that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, we didn't meet anyone else but Jetish got lost there in the mountains, whilst me and Sheqir stayed together until 7.00 p.m. with no food whatsoever. And then we reached his village, the village of Vojnik, on foot, and the village was in flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see anybody in the village of Vojnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, no one. After 11.00 p.m. we heard two elderly women, and we went to check who it was. So it turned out that there were two elderly women - I can't remember their names now - but they were able to recognise us, and they invited us to stay but we didn't. We returned to Sheqir's house, in fact, outside in the courtyard because the house was in flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does Vojnik have a school?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you arrived at Vojnik that day, did you see anyone in the school-yard or in the vicinity of the school?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: In the morning, an elderly woman who we called Halla Aza turned out, and I asked her for some water because we were covered in blood. And I said, May I have some water to wash my face because were the Serbs to see us they'd cut us to pieces with knives, being shot at would have been much, much easier. So we washed our faces, and at that stage we were able to see the police and the army installed in the yard to the school, and there were tanks in the vicinity as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were in the mountains, did you make any observations of the villages in the area around Izbica? Could you look into those villages and see the condition of those villages?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We were in a valley in the mountains, so all we were able to see was the smoke. We saw the black smoke billowing out of the village of Turjan. That's all we were able to see because we were in some kind of valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Or could we bring up 65 ter number 05260.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Thaqi, prepare a list of those persons, those men, in your group that you can recall who were killed on the morning of the 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I wrote a list of the people I was able to recognise. In the first group there were 10 or 11 whose names I didn't know because they came from some other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say the first group, you mean that group of 33 that you were with?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's the first group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is that the list of persons that you knew who were killed in your group?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like you, with the leave of the Court, to read out the names of those persons you remember were killed into the record starting from number 1.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. Regje Qelaj, Leqin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "Leqin" which is at the end, is that the village that he's from?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So for these names at the end of the names you put -- or after the surnames, I should say, you put the village that the person is from or was from?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to be also clear, the first name you have there as -- is a C with a diacritic, is that spelled sometimes in the Albanian language with a Q?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I -- I'm not sure? I'm not sure which are the Qs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Speaking about the first name.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think that's the way we write it, with a Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What's the next name?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Bel Durako, Broje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the next one?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Uke Uka Thaqi, Broje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the person you have here as Uke Uka Thaqi from your village of Broje, I think you mentioned earlier that he was one of the persons who died on top of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. It was Uka and Isuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to Uka, is he related to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: He is one of my next-door neighbours. We spent the night together that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is he related to you? Is he a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the relationship?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: My uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is he sometimes referred to as Uke Uka?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No. Uke Uka Thaqi, U-k.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is: Is it that sometimes his surname Thaqi is not used to refer to him, just Uke Uka, and excuse my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, without the Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I may just indicate to the Court that I'm just trying to clarify this name -- the names here with some of the names in the schedules to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you go to number 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Isuf Zeqa Shala, Broje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And number 5.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Hajriz -- no, Hazir Hoti, Jashanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Qerime Hoti, Jashanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see here it is written in the transcript with a Q for Qerime but you have put the C with a diacritic. Is that the same thing, it's interchangeable, the C and the Q here?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It's the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 7.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Demush Behrami, Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Number 8.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Mehmet Bajruku, Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Sokol Duraku, Broje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Number 10.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Tahir Hoti, Jashanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Number 11.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Hajriz Shala, Broje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Number 12.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Halit Haliti, Broje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Number 13.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Avdulla Duraku, Broje.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Muhamet Behrami, Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Number 15.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Muharrem Osmani, Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Number 16.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Azem Osmani, Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were Muharrem Osmani and Azem Osmani related?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They were three brothers. All three of them were killed. I did not write Hetem Osmani who belonged to the other group and who was disabled and who was also killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you same Hetem Osmani, I think you said Hetem, H-e-t-e-m, Osmani belonged to another group, he was --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: H, with an H, he was in another group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Was that another group from among the men who were gathered in the field that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, we were all in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. But when you say "another group," what do you mean? And I'm talking about Hetem. In which group or which other group was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Hetem was called when he was on his own. I did not see him, but this is what was described to me. They said that they had completed massacred him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, tell us what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: He was disabled. He was not able to walk. He had to use crutches. And from what I know, and I'm relating here what was told to me, they stabbed him with a knife and he used to shriek and he stopped shrieking only when the knife was pulled out. That's what some people who happened to be there told me. I did not see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did that happen on the same morning, on the 28th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, a bit later. He was caught when he was on his own but on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Number 17 on your list, if you could have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Brahim Kotorri, Vojnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And number 18.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Nuradin Behrami, Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And thank you for the list. I see that you have put in another column to the far right of the list --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I see you have put in a column to the far right of the list some numbers. What do these numbers designate?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: What village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. For example, if you look at number 1 you have a number 83 --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Forgive me, yes. That shows the age from what I was able to know. Some were 71, 64, 74, 54, 71, 57, 44, 63, 71, 67, 52, 56, 75, 72, 70, and 73, and the three of us who survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to page 2 of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this is all about. Could you just read what you have written here.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. "And the three of us who survived, Milazim Thaqi, Broje, 53 years of age, that is me; Sheqir Kotorri, Vojnik, 65; and Jetish Qallapeku, Shtupel, 63."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask that this be received in evidence and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00821, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, did you eventually return to the vicinity of Izbica where the killings occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: After three days, I was very unhappy, very sad, but we went back to bury these people that were killed. Only two we didn't bury that night. And we spent the night by the side of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, when you went back, the Serbs -- the Serbian army and police -- I withdraw that. When you went back, the police and members of the Yugoslav Army, were they still there, or had they left the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: After the massacre they left. Within four hours, all of them left. But I spent two days in Turiqevc. The third day I went to Kopiliq because I hadn't eaten anything for three days. And then a guy from Izbice came and said they are going to bury them today. And I said to him, How come, the Serbs are there? And he said, No, they left. That's how I came to go there and bury the victims. The KLA helped us and their family members, civilians as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall about how many victims were buried?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. That day we buried approximately 145 victims. Two, as I said, we couldn't bury that day; we buried them on the next day, early morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were all the victims buried by your group or were some taken away by their families?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Some families took their relatives and buried them elsewhere. I don't know how many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, while you were present at the burial, did you meet with other survivors from the remaining group of men or from the group of men who were killed that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That day, after we buried the victims, I met Jetish Qallapeki. I had some bread and some cheese with me, and he said, I haven't eaten anything for three days. So I gave him my bread and cheese, and I offered to bring him some water, but I warned him not to eat too much for fear he would suffer because of not having eaten for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe I should get right to the point. Did you discover what happened to the men that remained after your group of 33 were taken to the edge of the woods?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We saw everything ourselves when we went to the place of the event. Only 20 were not yet buried, and we started to carry them in groups and to bury them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So what had happened to these men? Did you discover what had happened to the remainder of the men that your group of 33 left behind? How did they die?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Just like us, they too were brought there in groups. How many in each group I don't know because they were all dead. I didn't have a chance to meet them. But I heard the shots, and we found the corpses there, and we counted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know Liri Loshi, Dr. Liri Loshi?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see him there that day during the burial?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I saw him that day and Thaqi -- [indiscernible] Thaqi had a camera, and he filmed everything that was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, when you said "filmed everything that was taking place," did they film the bodies of the dead men?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Where I was, we had already carried the corpses by the time, and I told them what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall if they filmed the bodies of the men who were killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you just said you showed them what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we look briefly at a videotape which is already in evidence. This is P00288. And I'd just like to show the witness a small part, two minutes of it or less than two minutes of it, a clip from minute 40.54 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- the person with the cap is myself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still have the clothes that I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what are you doing there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Here I'm telling them where I was lying on the ground, and that tree there, I -- at that tree there there was someone who tried to flee, but he was killed and he died there. And here where I am telling them at -- that at this place where all the corpses -- and that the person who shot us was 7 or 8 metres away in the meadow. Here we found the cartridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what are you showing them now as you crawl on the tape?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I'm telling them how we left. We mounted this area and that near the oak tree was the corpse and that we fled in the direction of the mountain. That the police and the army, they were round the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we could stop there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you and the other 33 men were taken off in a group to be shot, were the women and children still in the meadow or had they been sent away?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The women and the children, we were sitting on the meadow and the women and the children were asked to raise their three fingers and they killed -- they shot a horse in the presence of the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the women and the children, did they remain in the meadow that day or were they sent away? Did they leave?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They sent the women and the children immediately in some other direction, in the direction of Albania. And the two women I mentioned were the last in the group and they said that, We saw you when they took you to that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These are the two elderly women you met in Vojnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Your wife and children left in the direction of Albania with the other refugees?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: My wife and my children, that group from Izbice, went through Broje, Jashanice, Kline, Valjak, Gllogjan, to the church in Gllogjan which I don't know where it is. And they were told, Go back because the war is over so you can go back home. So they were on the run for seven days without eating anything. My daughter had young baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you reunited with them -- well, I suppose you were. When were you reunited with them?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: After 17 days I think we joined each other in Tushille.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Tushille is above Kopiliq, lower Kopiliq, between Laushe and Kopiliq i Ulet, lower Kopiliq. It is on the right side. And there were many refugees who took shelter there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you return to your village of Broje?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We didn't dare go back to Broje, not until the war was over, when NATO came, God help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you return to your home village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We returned to Broje on the 14th of June. We didn't find anything intact. The village was razed to the ground. There was no place we could sleep or stay in. Only some cherry trees were left. On the next day I was trying to do something in what had remained of my home, and two BBC journalists came there. They took me with them, and we went to Izbice. They saw themselves what had happened. They have levelled the grave-site --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to come to that, but -- well, let's get to it. You returned in mid-June to the area where you had buried these bodies, I take it, with the BBC journalists?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And described what was the condition of the grave-sites where you and the other Albanians had buried the dead men?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The place was levelled out, and I found an arm which they had excavated and also a leg and some wooden planks where we had written the names and last names of the victims. They were turned upside down and buried in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Apart from the leg and the arm, did you find any other bodies or body parts of the men you had buried?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No. To tell you the truth, no. Maybe there were some others, but where we looked we didn't find any other body parts. We only found those wooden planks that I mentioned buried in the grounds, and I got one of them and showed it to those journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you say that the place where you had buried the men was levelled out, could you just elaborate a little bit on that and tell us what you mean when you say it was levelled out.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: By this I want to say that -- they said initially, the Serbs, that Izbice village does not exist --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One minute, one minute --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That what happened in Izbice is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the condition of the ground where the people were buried. Why is it that you say it was levelled out?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The site seemed like it was dug with something. It was not only me there. The two journalists were there with me, and they saw it with their own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you notice anything about the area apart from the appearance that it had been dug? Could you observe when you went there that there were graves there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I didn't observe anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to return to the -- to what you said just now, that initially someone wanted to say that what happened in Izbica is not true. What do you mean by that? That persons wanted to say that what happened there was not true?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I meant that Belgrade said that it's all a lie what you say about what happened in Izbice, because they wanted to destroy all traces of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And from what you saw at the grave-site when you went there in mid-June, was that conclusion consistent with a view that they wanted to destroy all traces?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you see anything at the grave-site when you went there in mid-June that was consistent with the -- with any intention to destroy all traces?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This is what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what did you see at the grave-site, if anything, that might have been consistent with that intention? I'm just asking you now to tell us and describe what you say, if anything, at the grave-site in mid-June that indicated that to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: When we went back, there were no graves at all. But afterwards, the KFOR returned the corpses in batches from Batanice; and I went there to help in the burial in Vushtrri and another village whose names -- name I don't remember now. It is a live document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's return to the incident on the 25th -- sorry, on the 28th, the massacres in the morning, briefly. I'd like you to look at a chart and tell me if you can identify any of the patterns you see there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up 65 ter number 02375.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while it is being brought up, could I ask you, Mr. Thaqi, whether or not you noticed if the uniform that the commander wore, the person who told the other men that they knew what their duty was, whether it was a plain uniform or if it had a pattern.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It was a uniform with patterns like this one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There are four of them one there. Top right, top left, bottom right, bottom left? Which one?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This one, the top right. This one here, the top right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to make sure that we have it very clear, could you just put a number --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: -- the police one, but this other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Could you just put a 1 beside the uniform you say that the commander wore, a number 1.
