utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. The shooter, the man who escorted you to the hill -- edge of the woods and opened up with the machine-gun on the group of men, do you see any pattern like the one he was wearing there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which one is it? Don't draw, just tell us first. Just tell us which one it is first.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Under the 1 that I marked earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said you also saw an initial three men who asked for money and who burned a haystack. Do you see any uniform like the one that they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The first, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you put a number 2 there, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The uniform in number 2, how many men from the Serbian forces approximately were attired in that uniform at the field that morning?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I didn't count them, but I would say about 25 or so dressed in -- as policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it from what you just said that number 2 is a police camouflage pattern?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What colour do you call this, number 2?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We call it like -- I don't know how to say, like blue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In Albanian we call it yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I ask -- I'm not sure if that was from the witness or if the interpreter is trying to assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness mentioned the word "yellow" in Albanian, but by "yellow" they mean sometimes green, sometimes blue. That's why we hesitate. Say "yellow," maybe you can ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll just ask you again, Mr. Thaqi, number 2, what colour do you call that camouflage pattern?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We call it like yellow, like green, grass green. How can I say it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you that again because you have said two or three things. That's what I am getting on the interpretation. What do you call this colour, the wording you use to call this colour?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Like "e verdhe" which in English means like yellow, or like green grass green.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, as he had marked this, could it be given an exhibit number -- no, no, it's not in evidence just yet. So could this document be received in evidence and given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness also identified a third of the four colour patterns. I believe he said it was the one underneath the one numbered 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want that marked, perhaps, with a number 3 or are you happy to leave it as is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll be guided and ask him to mark that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- well, before you mark it, may I just make it clear where we are going now. Can you recall in your mind carefully the pattern of the uniform that the shooter was wearing, Mr. Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, it is this colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which one is it now?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The one under number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you put a number 3 there, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if there's anything else we could do with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00822, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up in e-court P316.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while -- before we bring it up, can I ask you, Witness, did some of the policemen you saw in the blue -- sorry, sorry, I withdraw that because it might be interpreted in a different way. Did some of the men you saw in the camouflage uniform that you marked number 2, did they have insignias on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, they did have badges on which "milicija" was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P316.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you -- there is someone here in this picture that I think you can see in uniform. Do you see the badge on the shoulder of --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall seeing this insignia or badge on the shoulder there that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the uniform -- the jacket, do you recall that pattern?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, the same. It's this kind of mixture, the police, the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up a little closer if we can, Mr. Usher, the vest that the police officer is wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look carefully at the pattern of the pockets at the bottom part of this vest, and I'd like you to recall the number 1 you marked on the chart before, can you perceive a difference between this pattern of camouflage that this policeman is wearing and the pattern of camouflage that the leader or commander was wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. This one here, the vest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is it? Tell us what you can say about it in relation to the man.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This pattern was in use within the Yugoslav Army as well as the police on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you showed us and marked number 1 in the previous chart as the pattern that the commander was wearing. Do you see a difference between this pattern here on the vest and the pattern that you showed us? Do you see a difference is the question, or are they the same?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They look the same to me in this vest, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you -- do you see the top right pocket of this vest, there's something written on it. Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I think it's written "milicija."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is for which of the armed forces, which of the armed organisations does "milicija" refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: What forces? It belongs to the police forces of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have completed the examination-in-chief. May it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Is that a convenient time, do you think, to have a break now, Mr. Djordjevic; or would you like to commence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the second break now and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are some questions for you now from Mr. Djordjevic. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Thaqi. My name is Dragoljub Djordjevic. I appear on behalf of the accused in this case. I have a few questions to put to you in order to clarify some matters that you have mentioned today and previously concerning the Izbica events.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, given that something is unclear to the Defence, and we believe it to be important in this case, I wanted to show a few different samples of colours to the witness in order for him to explain for him what colours those are, and I will have a few samples that I would like to put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, could you please look in my direction. Have a look at the piece of paper I'm holding in my hand and tell me what colour it is to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We call it "yellow," "e verdhe."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Green -- yellow, yellow. Would you also say that this is blue?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness answered in B/C/S saying:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [B/C/S Interpretation] Yes, blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will mark this with a 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask my assistant to hand it over to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What colour this, Mr. Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: [Albanian Interpretation] It's red.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will mark it with a 2, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What colour is this, Mr. Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It's like a grass colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will mark it with a 3, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: To conclude, what colour is this, Mr. Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It looks white to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You can have a look up close, and I will mark it with a 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's place that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to repeat starting with 1 through to 2, 3, and 4 and tell me what colours those are.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The one here is "e verdhe," "yellow," as we call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's the number 1?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Number 2 is red.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the number 3?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Grass colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Number 4?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: White.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you again about the paper number 1, the one you called "e verdhe" in Albanian. Do you also recognise that to be blue, what we call blue or perhaps not?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: We call it "e verdhe."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yellow. Since you said that the colour on the paper number 4 is white, I will try to do that exercise again. I will ask the usher to hand it over to you, and I would like to ask you what colour this piece of paper to you is. I would also like to ask the usher to replace the new sample with the old one, or rather, the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This is different than number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I do agree that it is a bit of a -- it is a stronger colour.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It's called "zelena" in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is there a word in the Albanian language for that colour, the paper number 4?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. It's similar to this one, to the off-white one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the Serbian word for the colour number 1?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: In Serbian it's called "zelena."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So both the 1 and the 4 are green?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will not press this any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will kindly ask the Chamber to have these samples admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we do, the first number 4 which is, I believe, an off-white and the second number 4 I would suggest that the second be marked 4A so that it can be distinguished. We should have all five.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The five samples will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And they will be assigned D00121, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, at the beginning of your testimony today you talked about the reasons why you and members of your family as well as your co-villagers left on the 25th or the 26th of March for Izbica, leaving your village, every last person did that. When asked by my learned colleague, Mr. Stamp, you cited massacres as the reason in Cirez, Likosane, Prekaz, and you said that those massacres took place in 1998. I will ask you again briefly whether you remember when those, as you term them, massacres took place in 1998, what month?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: You're going too fast for me. Are you asking me about the month when these occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The massacre in Qirez happened on the 28th of February, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a massacre in Likovac or Likosane?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, in Likoshan, yes. 28 persons, to what I know, were massacred there, not in L ikoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that the clashes that broke out in February 1998 were a direct consequence of the murder of two policemen on board a transport vehicle, the make was Lada, and that another two were wounded? Would you agree with me if I said that? It was an operation conducted by the Serbian police in order to save their colleagues who had been attacked by the KLA, two of which had been killed and two wounded.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Please, if one can tell the counsel to speak in shorter sentences, otherwise I'm not able to understand them. He speaks in long sentences, and I cannot remember everything he's putting into them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in February two policemen were killed, two Serb policemen; another two were seriously injured as they were riding in a transport Lada vehicle in Cirez and Likosane? Do you know of that event from February 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that. I heard that there was fighting. I know nothing else about it, and we went to bury the people that were massacred there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you will agree with me that there was fighting. Thank you. Another thing that I'm interested in is this: Did you testify in the case against the former Serbian President, late Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: On page 7146, line 10, when asked how many thousands of people approximately were at the meadow in Izbica you said "approximately 15 to 16.000." If I put to you that one of the survivors, Mustafa Dragaj, said that there were some 3.000 of us, and if I put to you that you, yourself, said today there were between 10 and 12.000 of us, what would be the exact number, the 3.000 referred to by Mr. Mustafa Dragaj; or between 10 and 12.000, as you said today; or 15 to 16.000 people as you put it a number of years ago in your testimony against the accused Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I didn't count them, neither did Mustafa count the people who were there. But most probably there were about 14 to 16.000 there. I wasn't a policeman or a soldier to count all of them. Some left, some remained there; how many left, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Out of the 14 to 16.000 people, as you said, can you tell me what was their make-up in terms of gender, age, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: As I said then, there were children of the age of 8 months, 1 year, up to elderly of the age of 100 and more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You have already stated that. I'm asking you now to tell us how many males were there in terms of percentage and how many women?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: 157, 160 altogether. Three of us survived. Nine survived there on the other side. So 12 of us survived. Now you make the math how many of us were men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell me that the rest were all women? And out of the total number of people on that meadow there were some 160 men?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. 160 men altogether, an old man Regje Duraku was killed as he was leaving Izbice. He was killed near the graveyard in Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where were the fathers, husbands, and brothers of those women, those tens of thousands of women or 15.000, where were they at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That I don't know. People were all out in the open, in the mountains. Some of the men were abroad. I don't know where all of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question for you, Mr. Thaqi, is this: You said that on that meadow in Izbica there were people from around 15 villages gathered there. Would you agree with me that there were 15.000 women and children in that village, and out of the men there were only the 157 of you? Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I didn't count how many people were there. It was impossible to count all of them there; but as far as men are concerned, we were about 160, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thaqi. My next question: Why did all of them gather in Izbica from all of the 15 villages? Why not a different location? What was the reason for them to all go to Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Well, the rumour amongst the population was that that was the safest area and that's why all the people came exactly there from all these different villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do all of those villages fall within the municipality of Srbica or were there some people from other villages as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: There were people from Kline municipality as well and from Skenderaj municipality, from these two municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there some people from Josanica, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Some were killed, some from Jashanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is that a third municipality, I mean does the village of Josanica fall within a third, another municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: It's in Kline municipality. It's not a third municipality. Only these two municipalities that I mentioned, Kline and Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me that that event in which the inhabitants of 15 villages all gathered in Izbica had to be the result of an agreement. Do you know who it was who decided that all of those people should go to Izbica out of the 15 villages, since as you testified yourself, people did not move about much due to danger?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That I don't know. The rumour amongst the population, as I said, was that that was the safest area, and that's why we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for the map of Kosovo showing Izbica to be put on the screen. I believe it is P819 on which I think the witness marked Izbica, Belanica, and some other villages. Could we also please zoom in on the part around Srbica municipality in the upper left-hand side corner. I think the map should be turned around. Actually, it's in the middle of the map, from Skenderaj to the east. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark Izbica on the map. You will be assisted by the usher.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: If you can wait for a moment, I cannot see it very well. Here is Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Will you mark it with 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, this is Izbice. Can you please enlarge it a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please help because the witness has still not made a mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Here, you can see it a little better now.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, Izbice, number 1; Vojnik is here; Turiqevc is a little bit lower; Kopiliq; Broje; and Tushille.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the witness now to use the same pencil that he used to mark Izbica to mark one by one the villages he sees here from which he knows people came to Izbica for safety, to say the name of each village before marking it. One of these is probably Vojnik. To the best of his recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Here is my village, Broje. Shall I underline it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Put a number 2 on it.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I will mark then Vojnik with number 2. It's closer to Izbice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That's number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any refugees from Turicevac? Can you see Turicevac if you can?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If you can, put number 3 there.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see your village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mark it with the next number, 4.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, can you see any other villages from which you know people came to Istok or north of Skenderaj, that is, Srbica or other places as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I cannot see Kline here. I cannot see Kline, Kline municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please, or rather, could, the Legal Officer expand the picture so we can see Kline, zoom out a little or maybe scroll down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can't move, Mr. Djordjevic. We lose it if we move.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell us then whether there were any refugees from Klina without marking it or maybe villages around Klina that you know about?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, there were people from Gllareve, but I cannot see Gllareve here on the map, and from Jashanice village which is also in Kline municipality. And from Rexheve village as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see Josanica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I think it's here, but I cannot see it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will tender this exhibit as it is. I will not ask for a new map. Thank you for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned D122.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, do you know who Bislim Zyrapi was?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that all the younger men from these villages and from the environs of Srbica did indeed flee but not to Izbica. It was three days before this unfortunate event. And none of them were with you, including the son of Mustafa Draga, who also said that his son went into the mountains, his younger son, and some people from the same village talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I don't understand you when you go on for a long time. If you can make your questions shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to rephrase to make the question easier. Is it the case that younger people, younger men, such as the son of Mustafa Draga, went into the mountains three days prior to the 28th, that is, around the 25th of March? That's why they were not in that meadow.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I don't know anything about Mustafa's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And concerning the younger people who were not there with you?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They were in the mountains, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was that something that was agreed with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: What kind of agreement with the KLA? What for?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will tell you that in his testimony, Bislim Zyrapi said that the KLA took care of the people, and accordingly the people agreed with the KLA when they would move and seek shelter elsewhere and that they, although poorly armed, were protecting their people. That's why I'm asking you. Is it the case that people moved from your village after that had been agreed with or ordered by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about what you're saying. To what I know, there was no agreement whatsoever with the KLA. We decided to leave, ourselves. And again, please, if you can put shorter questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at that time - that means the beginning of 1999 - did you know that the KLA existed, I mean you personally?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the KLA commander in the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Shaban Dragaj is?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I've heard of him, but I didn't see him at the time. I know him by sight; but at the time, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where is he from?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: He is from Leqin village, but I think he lives in Mitrovica or in Prishtina somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Have you just heard of him or do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I just heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell us all exactly what you heard of Shaban Dragaj?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Nothing special. They called him commander. I didn't hear anything else about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: From the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why did they call him commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Because perhaps he was a KLA leader or something like that. I don't know these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So you did hear that he was a commander. And now tell me, Mr. Thaqi, do you know the distance between his native village and Srbica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I don't know -- I know where Leqin is, but I don't know the distance between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your testimony earlier today - and you mentioned that also in certain statements to which I will come back later - that you had seen Serb forces coming from the direction of Josanica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This we saw in early March, in 1998; they came again in 1999 but then we left. We didn't see that with our own eyes, but we heard that they were coming from Kline and we left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Thaqi, that's exactly the event I'm asking you about. So you heard. You did not see Serbian forces coming from Josanica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I didn't see this with my own eyes. My house is in a valley and the villagers who live in the upper part of the village had seen them coming from that direction; and as I said, we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The villagers who saw that, who told you that the Serbian forces were coming, did they also tell you that there was shooting and there was some combat as the Serbian forces were arriving between them and members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The bullets were coming from the direction of Jashanice towards Broje, and we could hear the gun-fire ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: From Broje, not from your house but from the mountain, can you see Josanica with the naked eye?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: You can see the mill on the hill -- you can see it from the mill on the hill; but from the village where the houses are, you cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are there any settlements between Josanica and your village, Broje?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Jashanice borders Broje. There are no villages between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll agree with you on that. What is the distance between the centre of your village and the centre of Josanica?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Approximately some 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Given that we've agreed there are no settlements between Broje and Josanica, can you guess the reason for the fierce shooting that your villagers and you heard? What could be the reason?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was fighting between the KLA and the Serbian forces in that area on that occasion, that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I personally don't know that, but even there was -- even if there was fighting, we were in our own homes and they came to us and attacked us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Refki Thaqi and Elmi Thaqi are?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you related to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How are you related to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Close, close relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do they live far from you? How far are their houses from yours?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: About 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when all the villagers left Broje, were they also in the village, Refki and Elmi Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: These two left the village and went to Albania and they had given a false statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You know that they gave certain statements, to whom? Who kind of false statement did they make?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: When I was here for the second time, I was asked if I knew Refki and Elmi, and then they said that this is what they said, and I denied what they said. I told them that that all what they said was a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what exactly they said?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I don't remember what they had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I tell you they said in their statements, both of them, that they had seen Serbian forces come from the direction of Josanica. On that point your statements agree. You say you heard of it, and they say they saw it; but that involved, they say, great clashes with the Kosovo Liberation Army. Did they lie about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Most probably they lied about that. Personally I didn't see the fighting, and that's why I'm saying I didn't see any fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you don't know but you know that they lied about this, do you? Do you know that they lied when they said they had seen Serbian forces coming from the direction of Josanica which involved fighting with the KLA? I'm asking you about this second part.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I don't know if they lied or not. I assume that they didn't see this kind of fighting. They had given these statements in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do Refki and Elmi Thaqi live today in your village? Are they alive?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, Mr. Thaqi, did Refki and Elmi lie when they said that members of the KLA and the KLA commander for that area of Kosovo, the one you said you heard of as the commander, Shaban Draga, on the 24th of March, around 11.00 p.m., ordered all the young men in Izbica to leave and they did leave on the 25th of March around 3.00 a.m. Did they lie about that? Were you in Izbica at all on the 24th of March, that is, four days before the 28th?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I was at home on the 24th of March. On the 25th I was again at home. On the 24th the NATO bombing started. On the 26th, that was a Friday, we left early in the morning. As to the direction they took, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know whether their statement is true about this because you were not in Izbica at the time; will you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that on the 26th of March we went to Izbice. It was a Friday. I saw them later in Izbice, and after that I didn't see them anymore. They gave this statement some years later on, somewhere in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you, Mr. Thaqi, that they made their statement on the 30th of April, 1999, which is only two or three days after this massacre; and also on the 2nd May, 1999. But I have to go back away on this topic when you said, Oh, I know about them, they gave false statements. Since I understood you have no direct knowledge about any of these things, then what did they lie about? Why did you say they had given false statements when you know nothing about it? If you do know something, tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: They stated that the KLA was fighting in Izbice, not in Jashanice, but in Izbice, and that is a lie. There was no KLA in Izbice on that day when the massacre occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This seems to be a subject that you will be exploring for a little while, Mr. Djordjevic. I've been looking for a convenient break. This is probably it and we'll resume tomorrow at 9.00. Mr. Thaqi, we must finish for the day now but we continue tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, and we'll continue your evidence tomorrow morning. A court officer will give you further instructions overnight. So we look forward to seeing you again in the morning at 9.00, and we adjourn now for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of May, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.,
